 Xochitl Gomez Is Finding Her Voice in Hollywood
 Pop 
 Nov 11, 2026 @ 3:55 pm By Taylor Winter Wilson 
 From stepping into the Marvel Cinematic Universe as America Chavez in “ Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness “, to lending her voice to Gabby in the animated film “ The Cat in the Hat” , Xochitl Gomez is continuing to carve out her own path in Hollywood.
 But beyond the exciting roles and major productions, the young actress is learning the importance of creative freedom, representation, and protecting her peace.
 As she embraces a new chapter in her career, Gomez is discovering that finding her voice means more than simply stepping into the spotlight.
 In conversation with Galore , she opens up about bringing Gabby to life, working alongside some of Hollywood’s most recognizable talents, navigating the pressures of early success, and why staying true to herself remains her greatest priority.
 FEATURE INTERVIEW :
 This is your first major voice-acting role. What surprised you most about bringing Gabby to life without relying on the physical elements of on-camera acting?
 Xochitl Gomez: Performing with your voice is actually a huge part of on-camera acting. It’s just that you usually get to pair it with facial expressions and physicality, so all these things come together in a performance. But with animation, it’s up to the animators to interpret those things.
 Interestingly, during each voice-recording session, they had a camera set up to record our faces and upper torsos. When they animated our characters, they used the video to incorporate our facial expressions and body movements. There were moments when I was watching the movie and recognized my personal mannerisms, like when Gabby laughs!
 Gabby is described as a dramatic character. What parts of her personality do you relate to, and where do you see the biggest differences between you?
 Xochitl Gomez: I moved schools a lot when I was younger, so I can relate to Gabby in that way. But I felt those moves were opportunities to meet new friends, whereas Gabby feels like she’s leaving everything behind. I definitely had a more optimistic view at her age than Gabby does.
 How did you approach Gabby’s comedic timing and emotional range, especially when recording different versions of the same scene?
 Xochitl Gomez: With voice work, you have a chance to give various reads for each line or section of lines. The directors would ask for different reads because they’re piecing everything together and want all the options.
 So I did a range of reads, from high-energy to deadpan and bored, for many of the emotional sections. That way, they could play with the timing while editing. From there, they could choose which tone best fit the story and Gabby’s journey.
 You joined the project early in its development. How did your approach to Gabby evolve as the film began to take shape?
 Xochitl Gomez: I came on very early. I only had the script and a sketch of Gabby, so I was doing a range of reads just to give as many options as possible.
 When they finally had the movie halfway done, that’s when it started to come to life. From there, I worked with Alessandro and Erica, laying down all of Gabby’s lines to really nail down the emotions and delivery.
 When it got close to the final version, that’s when Bill and I had a couple of sessions together, which was super fun. I knew I needed to have a bunch of ideas for my lines because Bill is such an incredible improviser. You never know what’s coming!
 With a cast that includes Bill Hader, Quinta Brunson, Giancarlo Esposito, and America Ferrera, how did working alongside such talented performers influence your experience?
 Xochitl Gomez: I laid down my first recording three and a half years ago, so at the time, I had no idea who the other cast members would be apart from Bill. No one else had been cast at that point.
 We all met each other just recently because we recorded separately. The chemistry we have can be credited to great casting, and we naturally hit it off right away.
 I was lucky because Bill and I were able to record together twice, so I got to know him before press. I’ve known America for a few years through Latino events and outings. She’s someone I’ve always looked up to, so it was so cool to finally work with her and get to do press together.
 It’s a fantastic cast. Everyone is perfect for their part.
 What does it mean to you to bring Latina representation to a family-friendly animated film like The Cat in the Hat ?
 Xochitl Gomez: It’s wonderful that America, Tiago, and I got to be this family unit and the vehicle to bring these characters to the big screen.
 And, of course, we can’t forget that Latinos reliably show up at the movie theater more than any other group, so that’s a cool fact.
 The time is right, and I’m grateful to be part of this heartfelt journey.
 What do you hope audiences, particularly young Latina viewers, take away from Gabby’s story?
 Xochitl Gomez: I’d say that Gabby represents the universal stereotype of a gloomy teenager who believes her mom doesn’t understand her. What’s special about Gabby is her ability to change her perspective over the course of the film.
 How has working on The Cat in the Hat influenced your acting technique and the way you approach developing a character?
 Xochitl Gomez: The process of voicing Gabby has made me pay very close attention to voice and breath work in my acting technique.
 Gabby is written as a complex character, and my job was to give the team a range of emotions and reads in the booth so they could build her in a way that worked for the story.
 Judging by the crowd reactions that I’ve seen, I know they did a great job, and everyone loves it.
 How has your Latina identity influenced the roles you’re drawn to and the stories you want to tell?
 Xochitl Gomez: We are blessed to have very talented Latina storytellers, and I’m always looking for original material to bring to the table because that’s where great projects start—on the page.
 But truthfully, it’s actually so difficult to get studios on board. The projects I’m drawn to that have significant and layered Latina leads sometimes don’t make it past the initial stage.
 Really, getting to be part of any project with interesting character development is what it’s all about.
 Who are some of the women in the film industry you consider your personal sheroes?
 Xochitl Gomez: I’ll begin my list of sheroes right here with Quinta and America, two powerhouse women at the top of their game.
 It’s great to see talented women writing and directing, leading the rooms where decisions are made. I look up to them for the barriers they’ve broken, and I’m honored to be in this cast with them.
 You’ve spoken about how watching reshoots and stunt work as a child first sparked your interest in acting. How did that early experience shape your ambitions?
 Xochitl Gomez: It made a big impression on me because it was a big set, and it was so exciting. I had been doing youth theater, and to me, this was like a super big theater play with stunts and a huge crew.
 I knew right then that I wanted to be part of something like that. It helped me understand what the job looked like and what happens once you get there.
 I was like, all these people are here doing this job, and I can too.
 Your role as America Chavez in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness introduced you to a much larger audience. How did that level of visibility change your experience navigating Hollywood?
 Xochitl Gomez: I was so excited to be part of the Marvel franchise. After the movie came out, there were a lot of assumptions that people made about me, so that was an unexpected roadblock.
 But truthfully, the hardest thing was casting. They would say I’m too recognizable or assume I’m too expensive, so getting auditions back then was a challenge.
 That was a weird time, and I needed to pivot away from disappointment. Then Dancing with the Stars came along, and it changed my perspective. I got to throw myself into that world and just wait for the right acting project to find me.
 As your career continues to evolve, you’ve emphasized the importance of feeling safe and finding joy in your work. How are those priorities shaping the opportunities you pursue?
 Xochitl Gomez: By prioritizing my safety and joy, I’ve realized how vital that is for my personal well-being.
 I don’t ever want to accept a role where either of those is compromised. Taking breaks and slowing down helps me be the best version of myself.
 It’s important to me that I enjoy the work that I do.
